title: Bhishma's fall
hook: losing every day to their own grandsire, the Pandavas walk across the field at night to ask him how he can be killed

segments.voice: Yesterday Krishna twice leapt from the chariot and ran at Bhishma, and twice Arjuna pulled him back. Your line: to be killed by you would be an honor. And the old man is still standing.

Night, and the Pandava camp is quiet in the wrong way. Another day has gone to Bhishma, the commander of the other side and the elder these brothers grew up calling grandsire. Yudhishthira can't see a way through. Then he remembers the first morning, when he walked over to Bhishma unarmed. Bhishma told him then that he could not fight for the Pandavas but would still give them counsel, and that the question of how he could be beaten should be asked again another time. So the brothers set their weapons aside, and with Krishna they walk across the dark field to the enemy's tent.
screen: `ANOTHER DAY LOST TO BHISHMA.` → `A PROMISE OF COUNSEL.` → `ACROSS THE FIELD AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Bhishma doesn't reach for a sword. In Ganguli's English, he welcomes them, asks why they've come, and offers to do whatever he can for them. Yudhishthira asks the question out loud. How can you be defeated? How can we win, when you stand in the way? It's an unbearable thing to ask a man you love. And Bhishma answers it. As long as he holds his bow, no one can bring him down. But there is a warrior he will not fight. Shikhandi, Drupada's son, was born a daughter, and Bhishma has vowed never to raise a weapon against one he counts as a woman. Put Shikhandi in front, he tells them. Let Arjuna shoot from behind. Then the brothers walk back across the field, and the text lets us hear Arjuna come apart. He remembers being a small boy, climbing into Bhishma's lap, getting dust on his clothes, and calling him father. And Bhishma gently correcting him: not your father, child, your father's father. How can I kill him, Arjuna asks. Krishna steadies him: Arjuna has already promised to fight, and Bhishma himself has told them the way. The enemy commander is also the family elder. He tells the truth even when the truth is his own death. And the grandson who must aim at him once sat in his lap. The text doesn't make any of it easy.
screen: `THE ENEMY WELCOMES THEM` · `"HOW CAN YOU BE DEFEATED?"` · `SHIKHANDI IN FRONT` · then, large: `A BOY IN HIS GRANDSIRE'S LAP`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose counsel you'd trust even when it's hard to hear: a teacher, an elder, an old friend. Breathing in, see their face; breathing out, quietly name one question you'd bring them, the way the brothers brought theirs across the field. If you pray, that question can become your prayer.
Bhishma's fall. Tonight it begins with a question asked in his own tent, and an honest answer that he gives against himself.
Your line: put Shikhandi in front. The counsel he promised, given against himself. That's day eight hundred twenty-seven.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Pandavas found Bhishma's weak spot.

what a scholar hears: the scene sets duty against love on both sides: Bhishma's honesty kills him, and Arjuna's promise to fight makes him the one who must do it.

chat.says: Wait, Bhishma told his enemies how to beat him? Why would he?
options: He'd promised Yudhishthira counsel, and told the truth, though it meant his death.
He thought Shikhandi was far too weak to ever reach him anyway.
He wanted to trap them, so he gave them a false plan on purpose that night.
chat.meaning: Bhishma had promised Yudhishthira counsel. Asked at night how he could be defeated, he named Shikhandi, a warrior he would not fight.

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli that the brothers lay aside armor and weapons for the visit, that Krishna goes with them, and that Bhishma's counsel names Shikhandi with Arjuna behind him.

Confirm Arjuna's memory (climbing into Bhishma's lap as a child, calling him father, Bhishma replying he is his father's father) and the wording 'one he counts as a woman' for Bhishma's vow regarding Shikhandi.
Bhishma is called grandsire throughout; he is strictly the Pandavas' great-uncle.
